inline.s: Later, at Ciyun Temple, I met an old man with a long beard and an extraordinary countenance, who seemed almost to float like an immortal. I bowed to him respectfully. The old man said to me, “You are by destiny a man of official life; next year you will pass the xiucai examination. Why do you not study?” I told him my reason for not studying, and asked his surname and where he lived. The old man said, “My surname is Kong, and I am from Yunnan. I received the orthodox transmission of the Imperial Ultimate numbers from Master Shao Yong of the Song dynasty. Above, I know whether a nation will flourish or decline; below, I know each person's good fortune and misfortune. By the fixed number, I am to transmit the Imperial Ultimate numbers to you.” Thereupon I invited him to my home and reported the matter to my mother, who said, “Treat him well.”

We tested Mr. Kong's Imperial Ultimate numbers, and everything he calculated, down to the finest detail, proved accurate one by one. This showed that Mr. Kong foresaw things as if by divine insight, and since he said I would pass the xiucai examination next year and afterward enter official life, I conceived the wish to study. I went to discuss it with my elder cousin Shen Cheng, who said, “Mr. Yu Haigu has opened a school at the home of Shen Youfu; it would be very convenient for me to send you there as a boarding student.” So I took Mr. Yu as my teacher.

Mr. Kong used the Imperial Ultimate numbers to calculate my prospects in the xiucai examination of the following year. He said that, sitting the county examination as a tongsheng, I would place fourteenth; in the prefectural examination, seventy-first; and in the provincial examination, ninth. When I went to the examinations the next year, the placings in all three were exactly as he had calculated, and so I passed and became a xiucai.

Mr. Kong also calculated the good and ill fortune of my whole life. He said, “In such a year you will place such a rank in the examinations; in such a year you will receive the government stipend; in such a year you will become a tribute student. In a certain year after that you will be selected to serve as county magistrate in Sichuan, and after three and a half years in office you ought to resign and return home. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month of your fifty-third year, at the hour of the ox, you will die in your own bedroom — and alas, you will have no son.” I wrote down Mr. Kong's words one by one and carefully stored them in my mind.

From then on, the placings in every examination and the order of every promotion were exactly as Mr. Kong had calculated. In one thing only did he differ: he reckoned that I would become a tribute student when my stipendiary rice reached ninety-one dan and five dou; yet when my rice had reached only a little over seventy dan, Commissioner Tu, the education commissioner, approved my promotion to tribute status. I privately wondered whether it would go through, and in the end the county's petition was indeed rejected by Mr. Yang, the acting commissioner who succeeded him.

It was not until the year dingmao that Commissioner Yin Qiuming, the education commissioner, saw the examination papers I had drafted and sighed, saying, “These five policy essays are like five memorials submitted by a great minister to the throne. How can we let a scholar of such deep and thorough learning be buried in obscurity all his life!” He therefore approved my promotion to tribute student in accordance with the county's earlier petition; and when the stipendiary rice I had eaten was reckoned together, it came to exactly ninety-one dan and five dou.

I therefore became all the more convinced that advancement and obscurity are appointed by fate, and that whether things come early or late has its fixed time. And so my heart grew cold and I sought nothing more.
After becoming a tribute student I went to Beijing, and during the year I spent there I sat in quiet meditation all day long, reading neither essays nor books.

In the year jisi I returned to Jiangnan and went to study at the Imperial Academy in Nanjing. Before enrolling, I first went to call on Chan Master Yungu and met him at Qixia Temple in the Sheshan hills. The two of us sat facing each other in a single room, and for three days and three nights I did not once doze off or fall asleep. Chan Master Yungu asked, “The reason a person cannot become a sage is only that deluded thoughts entangle him. Yet you have sat for three days and three nights without giving rise to a single deluded thought. How is this possible?”

I replied, “My fate has already been settled by Mr. Kong. Honor and disgrace, death and life, all have their fixed number. Even if I wished to have deluded thoughts, there would be nothing to think about.”

Chan Master Yungu laughed and said, “When I saw you sitting in stillness for three days and three nights with your eyes unclosed and not a deluded thought arising, I took you for someone quite extraordinary. It turns out you are only an ordinary man.”

I asked him why he called me an ordinary man. Chan Master Yungu said, “Ordinary people cannot yet reach the state of no-mind; they are forever seizing upon outer conditions and turning things over in their thoughts, and so in the end they are bound by yin and yang and inevitably have a fixed fate. But it is only the fate of ordinary people that is fixed. One of the utmost goodness, by doing deeds of the utmost goodness, turns his destiny for the better, and so the fixed number cannot hold him. One of the utmost wickedness, by doing deeds of the utmost wickedness, turns his destiny for the worse, and so the fixed number cannot hold him either. For these twenty years you have been wholly calculated by Mr. Kong, and you have not moved your fate by so much as a hair. If you are not an ordinary man, what are you?”
I asked, “Then can this fixed fate be escaped?”

Chan Master Yungu said, “‘Fate is made by oneself; blessing is sought by oneself.’ The truth set forth in the Book of Songs and the Book of History is indeed an excellent teaching. Our Buddhist scriptures say, ‘Seek wealth and honor, and you obtain wealth and honor; seek sons and daughters, and you obtain sons and daughters; seek long life, and you obtain long life.’ This is absolutely true. For the prohibition of false speech is the gravest and most essential precept in Buddhism; how could the Buddhas and bodhisattvas deceive people with false words?”

I went on to ask, “Mencius said, ‘Seek, and you will obtain it, because what is sought lies within myself.’ Virtue and benevolence rest with oneself, and I can obtain them if I strive. But rank, fame, wealth, and honor do not rest with me; if others do not grant them, how can I obtain them?”

Chan Master Yungu said, “Mencius spoke truly; it is you who have understood him wrongly. Have you not seen how the Sixth Patriarch Huineng says in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, ‘All fields of blessing are within each person's own mind; seek within your own mind, and where sincerity reaches, you will surely obtain’? To seek within oneself means to cut off evil and accumulate goodness. Then one gains virtue and benevolence within, and rank, fame, wealth, and honor without — gaining both within and without, and such seeking is effective. But if one does not reflect on one's own faults and does not strive to cut off evil and accumulate goodness, but merely gallops outward in pursuit, then even with schemes and stratagems, whether one obtains anything is wholly decided by fate. The usual result is that one gains no virtue or benevolence within and no rank or wealth without, losing both within and without: such seeking is of no use.”

Seeing that I still did not quite understand, Chan Master Yungu, prescribing the remedy to fit the illness, turned the conversation and asked me, “What exactly did Mr. Kong calculate your life would be?” I told him truthfully. Chan Master Yungu said, “Weigh it for yourself: do you deserve to pass the examinations and take office? Do you deserve to have a son?”

I reflected for a long while before answering, “I do not. Those who pass the examinations and take office mostly have the countenance of good fortune. I was born with scant blessing, and I cannot sustain a good mind and diligently do good deeds to thicken it. Moreover, I have no patience for troublesome matters, my measure is narrow, I am forever overshadowing others with my cleverness, and I indulge my temper and speak lightly and wildly. All of these are marks of scant blessing — how could I pass the examinations and take office! Filthy ground breeds living things, while clear water often holds no swimming fish; I was excessively fastidious about my own purity, to the point of being cold and inhuman — this is the first reason I ought to have no son. Harmony can give life to all things, yet I am fond of losing my temper — this is the second reason I ought to have no son. Benevolence is the root of unending life, while a cruel and unkind heart is the cause of barrenness; I cared only for guarding my own name and honor and could seldom give up myself to save others — this is the third reason I ought to have no son. Much talk drains the vital breath — this is the fourth reason I ought to have no son. Fondness for drink scatters the spirit — this is the fifth reason I ought to have no son. I often sat through the whole night in meditation without knowing how to conserve my primal vitality and nourish my spirit — this is the sixth reason I ought to have no son. As for my other faults and evils, they are still many, and I could not list them all.”

Chan Master Yungu said, “You just said, ‘Those who pass the examinations and take office mostly have the countenance of good fortune.’ In truth, it is not only rank and office: wealth and honor, and the bearing of sons, all depend on merit and virtue. Whoever in this world enjoys a fortune of a thousand pieces of gold must be a person with the reward of a thousand pieces of gold; whoever enjoys a fortune of a hundred pieces must be a person with the reward of a hundred; whoever starves to death must be a person who deserves to starve. Heaven simply carries out, exactly as it is, the fortune or misfortune each person already has — where would it add the least intention of its own? Take the matter of having sons. One who has accumulated hidden virtue for a hundred generations will surely have descendants for a hundred generations to preserve it; one who has accumulated hidden virtue for ten generations will surely have descendants for ten generations to preserve it; one who has accumulated hidden virtue for three generations or two will surely have descendants for three generations or two to preserve it. And those whose line is cut off — it is all because they have not accumulated hidden virtue!”

Now that you know where your faults lie, you must thoroughly rid yourself of the failings that have kept you from passing the examinations and from having a son. You must accumulate hidden virtue; you must be tolerant of others; you must be gentle and loving; you must cherish your spirit. Let all that belongs to the past be gone — pay it no more heed, as though you had died yesterday. Let all that belongs to the future begin anew, as though you were born today; and this reborn self of yours is a wholly new body of benevolence, righteousness, and virtue.

Even a body of flesh and blood has its fixed fate; how much more should a body of benevolence, righteousness, and virtue be able to move Heaven! The Taijia says, ‘Calamities sent down by Heaven may still be avoided; calamities you bring upon yourself you must surely suffer.’ Mr. Kong calculated that you would not pass the examinations and would not have a son: these are calamities sent down by Heaven, and they may still be escaped. Now, if you enlarge your noble character, diligently practice good deeds, and accumulate much hidden virtue, that is blessing you make for yourself — how could you fail to enjoy it?”

The Book of Changes plans for the noble man how to pursue good fortune and avoid misfortune. If the decree of Heaven were fixed and could not be changed, how could good fortune be pursued and misfortune avoided? In its very first chapter it says, ‘The family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of blessings to leave to its descendants, and so its descendants will certainly flourish.’ Do you believe what I have said to you?”

Chan Master Yungu's words were like a thunderclap that wakes the deaf, and I felt as though I had woken from a dream. Believing him without a trace of doubt, I bowed respectfully and accepted his teaching. Thereupon, before the Buddha, I repented with all my heart, confessing all my past faults and evils without the least concealment; and I wrote out a petition, first seeking to pass the provincial examination, and vowed to perform three thousand good deeds to repay the grace of Heaven and Earth and of my ancestors.

Seeing that I had vowed to perform three thousand good deeds, Chan Master Yungu brought out a ledger of merit and demerit and showed it to me, telling me to record everything I did, day by day: good deeds counted as merit and entered, evil deeds counted as demerit and deducted. He also taught me to hold the mantra of Cundi, so as to guarantee that the remaking of my fate would surely succeed.

Chan Master Yungu said to me, “Those who make a profession of drawing talismans have a saying: ‘If the talisman you draw is not efficacious, even the ghosts and spirits will laugh at you.’ The secret of an efficacious talisman is this: when drawing it, do not stir a thought. When you take up the brush to draw the talisman, first set down everything in your mind, gather your attention completely, and do not let even the finest thought arise. At the moment when no thought is present, make a single dot; this dot is called the opening of the foundation of chaos, and it lays the basis for the whole talisman. From there, drawing it through in one continuous stroke without giving rise to a thought in the process, the talisman will be efficacious. Whenever one prays to Heaven or seeks to remake one's fate, one must enter the state of concentrated absorption free of stray thoughts, and thereby attain spiritual response.

To be undivided toward favorable and adverse circumstances — only then can the mind settle, only then can one be at peace in poverty and delight in the Way; this is the foundation for remaking one's fate. Confucius's disciple Yan Hui was the model of finding peace in poverty and joy in the Way. Confucius praised him, saying, ‘How worthy was Hui! A single basket of rice, a single gourd of water, dwelling in a mean lane — others could not have borne the sorrow, yet Hui did not let his joy be altered. How worthy was Hui!’

When Mencius set forth the principle of remaking one's fate, he said, ‘a short life and a long life are not two.’ And yet a short life and a long life are utterly different things! But when we do not stir our minds to love and hate, to take and reject — no thinking, no deliberating — where is there any short life or long life? Spelled out in detail: only when abundance and scarcity are seen as no different can a fate of poverty be turned into a fate of wealth; only when hardship and success are seen as no different can a fate of hardship be turned into a fate of success; only when a short life and a long life are seen as no different, with life and death set outside one's concern, can a fate of early death be turned into a fate of long life. In this human world, life and death are the weightiest matter of all, and that is why Mencius spoke only of being without discrimination between a short life and a long life. In fact, being without discrimination toward all favorable and adverse circumstances — wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness, success and hardship, long life and short life — is all contained in that one phrase.

As for ‘cultivating oneself and awaiting it,’ this is the matter of accumulating hidden virtue and praying to Heaven. As for ‘cultivating,’ it means that all one's own faults and evils should be corrected and removed; as for ‘awaiting,’ it means waiting until the work of self-cultivation is deep, and then one's fate will of itself improve. One must not harbor the least inordinate hope, nor may one pursue and curry favor; if any such thing arises, it must be utterly cut off and removed. Reaching this state, one then returns to the origin and goes back to the source, revealing the original face of purity, wisdom, and great power. This is true learning!

You cannot yet reach the state of ‘no affairs in the mind, no mind in affairs,’ but you may recite the mantra of Cundi to cultivate the mind and reach a state of concentrated absorption free of stray thoughts. When reciting the mantra, do not keep count and do not let it be interrupted. When your recitation has become thoroughly familiar, then within reciting there is no reciting, and within not reciting there is reciting; when you realize and enter the state of no-thought and yet no absence of thought, the mantra you recite will be efficacious, and spiritual response will appear of itself.”

My former style name was Xuehai. That very day I changed it to Liaofan, meaning 'no longer an ordinary man,' for I had already understood the principle of establishing one's own fate and no longer wished to be an ordinary man tossed about by destiny.

From then on I was careful and circumspect all day long, and felt myself different from before. Formerly I had been careless and self-indulgent; now I was reverent and cautious, fearing only that I might do wrong. Even where no one was present, I was ever afraid of offending Heaven, Earth, and the spirits; and when I met people who hated or slandered me, I could of myself accept it calmly and peaceably without taking account of it.

The next year I went to the preliminary examination held by the Ministry of Rites. Mr. Kong had calculated that I would place third, but I unexpectedly placed first: his words had begun to fail. And in the provincial examination that autumn I passed and became a juren.

In the early days of reforming my faults and accumulating goodness, though I strove very hard, what I ought to do still came with a certain reluctance, and my mind still held stray thoughts; examining my words and deeds, I found many remaining failures. Sometimes I saw a good deed and did it, but without pressing forward courageously; sometimes when the moment came to save someone, my mind still wavered; sometimes I forced myself to do good in action while my speech was often at fault; sometimes, while sober, I could still hold myself in check, but once drunk I ran wild. Merit offset demerit, and many days passed in vain with no goodness accumulated.

From the year jisi, when I made my vow, until the year jimao — more than ten years in all — I finally completed the three thousand good deeds I had pledged. At that time I was accompanying Li Jian'an through the pass on official business and had no chance to dedicate the merit. It was only the following year, after I had returned to my home in the south, that I asked the venerable monks Xingkong, Huikong, and others to perform the dedication at the East Pagoda Chan Hall.

When the dedication was finished, I made a vow to seek a son, and pledged to perform three thousand good deeds in return. The following year my son Tianqi was born. For every good deed I did I at once noted it down in writing; your mother, who could not write, would mark each good deed she did with a red circle stamped on the calendar with a goose quill — whether giving food to the poor or buying living creatures to set free — sometimes as many as a dozen circles in a single day. Three years passed, and by the eighth month of the year guiwei all three thousand good deeds I had pledged were completed. So I again asked the venerable Xingkong and the others to perform the dedication in our courtyard at home.

On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of that year I made a further vow to pass the jinshi examination, pledging to perform ten thousand good deeds in return. Three years later, at the age of fifty-one, I passed the jinshi examination and was appointed by the Ministry of Personnel as magistrate of Baodi County. I prepared a small ruled notebook and named it 'The Compilation of Mind-Cultivation.' Each morning, before going to the hall to attend to business, I had a servant take this notebook to the gatekeeper and set it on my desk, so that whatever good or evil I did that day, however trifling, was recorded one by one. In the evening I set a table in the courtyard, put on my official robes, lit incense, and, following the example of Zhao Yuedao, reported to the Lord of Heaven each thing I had done during the day.

Your mother, seeing that we had not done many good deeds, would knit her brows and say, “When we lived at home I helped you do good deeds, and so you were able to complete the three thousand you had pledged. Now you have pledged ten thousand good deeds, and here we live in the deep inner quarters of the magistrate's residence with nothing good to do — when will they ever be finished?” That very night I happened to see a divine being in a dream, and I told him why the ten thousand good deeds were so hard to complete. The divine being said, “By the single matter of reducing the grain levy, the ten thousand good deeds you pledged are already accomplished.”

It turned out that the grain levy in Baodi County was two fen, three li, and seven hao per mu of land. Seeing that the burden on the people was too heavy and their lives unbearably hard, I investigated the actual circumstances, reported to my superiors, and memorialized the court, and in the end the levy was reduced to one fen, four li, and six hao; so the reduction of the grain levy did indeed take place. What astonished me considerably was that the divine being knew of it and said it could count for ten thousand good deeds; whether it could truly count for so much, I was somewhat in doubt.

It happened that Chan Master Huanyu came from Mount Wutai, so I told him of the dream and asked whether it could be believed. Chan Master Huanyu replied, “If the good heart is true and earnest, then a single good deed can count for ten thousand good deeds — how much more so this reduction of the grain levy for the whole county, a great matter that brought blessing to thousands and tens of thousands of people!” Hearing his words, I became certain that I had fulfilled my vow of ten thousand good deeds, and at once donated my salary silver, asking him to feed ten thousand monks at Mount Wutai and perform the dedication for me.
Mr. Kong had calculated that I would die at fifty-three. Though I never prayed for long life, that year passed for me in peace and safety, and this year I am already sixty-nine.

The Book of History says, 'Heaven is hard to trust; the mandate is not constant.' It also says, 'The mandate is not fixed.' These words are all true and not false. From this I know that whoever says blessing and calamity are brought about by oneself speaks the words of sages and worthies, while whoever says blessing and calamity are bestowed by Heaven speaks the common talk of the world.

Your fate — who knows how it will turn out. Even if your destiny is to be honored and exalted, you should always think of decline and neglect; even if your times run smoothly, you should always think of adversity; even if you are prosperous before your eyes, you should always think of poverty; even if people love and respect you, you should be careful and circumspect and always think with fear; even if your family is of high repute, you should always think of yourself as lowly; even if your learning is rather superior, you should always think of it as shallow and meager.

Thinking far ahead, you should spread abroad the grace and virtue of your ancestors; thinking close at hand, you should make up for your parents' faults and errors with good deeds. Looking upward, think of repaying your country's grace; looking downward, think of creating blessings for your family. Outwardly, think of relieving the urgent distress of others; inwardly, think of guarding against your own evil thoughts.

You must know your own faults every day and correct your own faults every day. If for one day you do not know your faults, then for that day you rest content in the belief that you have none; if for one day you have no fault to correct, then for that day you make no progress. There are truly many clever and gifted people in the world; the reason their virtue does not grow better with cultivation and their undertakings do not grow greater is nothing but those four words, 'muddling along for present comfort,' which fritter away a whole lifetime.

The teaching on establishing one's own fate that Chan Master Yungu transmitted is the most refined, the most profound, the most true, and the most upright of principles. You must study it closely and read it again and again, come to realize its meaning for yourself, and then carry it out with all your heart and strength. Above all, do not let these fine years pass in vain!

blocks.text: Part Two. The Method of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Many of the great officers of the Spring and Autumn period could foretell a person's fortune or misfortune from his speech and bearing, and they were never wrong, as may be seen throughout the Zuo Commentary, the Guoyu, and other such records. The omens of good and ill fortune for the most part sprout in the mind and then pervade the whole body, so that they show in a person's speech and bearing. Those whose speech and bearing are steady and generous often obtain blessing; those whose speech and bearing are frivolous and mean often meet with calamity. Yet worldly people, blind as though their eyes were open, cannot see it, and so they say that fortune and misfortune are uncertain and cannot be foretold. Those great officers, however, by virtue of their utmost sincerity, were in accord with the mind of Heaven and so could perceive these omens. When they saw good omens, they knew beforehand that the person would obtain blessing; when they saw bad omens, they knew beforehand that he would meet with calamity.

blocks.text: 1. The Three Minds of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Faults and evils are the root of ruined blessing and coming calamity. Now, if one wishes to obtain blessing and keep misfortune at a distance, then before speaking of doing good and creating blessing, one must first speak of how to reform one's faults. But to reform one's faults, one must do the following:

First, one must arouse the mind of shame. Consider: the sages and worthies from ancient times and I are all alike great men. Why is it that after a hundred generations people still learn from them, while my whole life is like a roof tile shattered on the ground, worth nothing at all?

To wallow in the passions and desires of this dusty world, secretly doing all manner of things one ought not to do, and still to think that others do not know, proud and unashamed — thus day by day to sink toward the level of beasts without knowing it oneself: among the things in this world that are shameful, none is greater than this! Mencius said, 'The greatest and most essential thing for a person is to know shame.' For if one knows shame, one will strive to reform one's faults, one's virtue will be renewed day by day, and by persisting one may become a worthy or a sage. If one does not know shame, one will give free rein to one's will, gradually lose one's human character, and sink to the level of beasts. Therefore knowing shame is the key to reforming faults.

Second, one must arouse the mind of awe. Heaven and Earth are above us, and ghosts and spirits are hard to deceive; though others may not see my faults and evils, Heaven, Earth, and the spirits see them perfectly clearly.

Nor is that all. Even in a private room or a dark corner, everything I do is watched by the eyes of the spirits and pointed at by their fingers, as though in the broad light of day. However secretly I conceal it and however cleverly I gloss it over, the desire in my heart has long since shown itself, and in the end it is hard to deceive either myself or others; once someone sees through me, I am not worth a penny! How can one fail to keep a mind of reverence always present?

Nor is that all. So long as a person still has a breath left, even the greatest of crimes may still be repented and reformed. There was once a man who did evil all his life, yet repented as he lay dying, and by the arising of a single good thought he met a good end — because that single thought was utterly sincere and piercingly earnest, and so it could wash away the evil of a lifetime. It is like a deep valley dark for a thousand years: let a single lamp shine into it, and the darkness of a thousand years is wholly dispelled. Therefore, whether a fault is long-standing or newly committed, it is most precious once it is reformed.

But the affairs of this dusty world are hard to foresee, and this body of flesh is easily lost; when the breath does not return, even if one wishes to reform one's faults, there is no way left to do so. Having failed to reform them in time, one dies, and in this world of the living one bears a bad name for a thousand or a hundred years; even filial sons and compassionate grandsons cannot wash it away for him. In the world below, for a thousand or a hundred kalpas he sinks into the hells and suffers retribution; even sages, worthies, Buddhas, and bodhisattvas cannot rescue him. How can one fail to be afraid?

Third, one must arouse the mind of courage. The reason people do not reform their faults is mostly that they delay and shrink back. I must rouse myself with determination, without hesitation and without waiting. A small fault is like a fine thorn in the flesh — hard to bear, hard to endure — and one draws it out at once. A great fault is like a poisonous snake biting one's finger: to preserve one's life, one cuts off the finger at once, unafraid of the pain. There must be not the slightest hesitation or lingering; this is why swift and resolute action is so very effective.

Once one possesses the mind of shame, the mind of awe, and the mind of courage, one can reform a fault as soon as it arises. When faults and evils meet these three minds, they are like thin ice in spring meeting the sun: is there any fear that they will not melt away?

blocks.text: 2. The Three Methods of Reforming Faults

inline.s: Now, a person's faults and evils may be reformed at the level of the deed, at the level of principle, or at the level of the mind; because the methods differ, their results differ as well.

For example, if one formerly killed living beings, one now forbids oneself to kill; if one formerly lost one's temper and scolded others, one now forbids oneself to be angry: this is reforming at the level of the deed. To reform at the level of the deed is to force oneself from the outside not to transgress; it is a hundred times harder than reforming from within, and moreover the root of the disease remains. When it is stamped out in the east, it springs up in the west: this is not a way to uproot faults and evils completely.

One who is skilled at reforming faults will always make the principle clear before forbidding himself a thing. For example, if the fault lies in killing living beings, then reflect: the Lord on High delights in life and hates slaughter, and all animals love their own lives and wish to live. How can the heart be at peace when one kills them to feed oneself? Moreover, when they are killed they suffer the butcher's knife and are plunged into boiling pots and oil cauldrons, every kind of pain piercing to the marrow; while for oneself, even if the table is spread with every delicacy and the rarest seafood, once it has passed the throat no flavor can be distinguished at all. Plain vegetables and soup can fully satisfy hunger — why must one kill them and so diminish one's own share of blessing?

Reflect further: creatures with flesh and blood and breath all have a spirit and awareness; since they have a spirit and awareness, they are one of us. Even if I cannot cultivate such lofty virtue as to make them respect me and draw near to me, how can I kill them day after day and make them hate and resent me without end? As soon as this thought arises, one will grieve over such food and be unable to eat it.

For example, if one is given to anger, one must reflect: if another's ability falls short and a matter is not handled well, by all reason I ought to pity him. If he offends me unreasonably, the fault is his — why should I flare up and torment myself? Therefore there is truly nothing to be angry about.

Reflect further: in all the world there is no such thing as a hero who thinks himself always right, nor such a thing as learning that lays the blame on others. When a matter fails, it is always because one's own virtue is not well cultivated and cannot move others to support me and join me in finishing it with one heart.

Whenever I meet with anything contrary, I look for the cause entirely in myself. In this way, all slander becomes a fine opportunity to temper me, raise me up, and bring me to accomplishment; I have not even time to be grateful — how could I be angry?

Moreover, if others slander and attack me, so long as I do not grow angry, then however fierce their bluster, it is no more than raising a torch to burn the empty sky, where there is nothing to burn, and the fire goes out of itself. But if I grow angry when slandered and attacked, then even if I strain my wits to argue cleverly, I am only spinning a cocoon that binds me, bringing on endless entanglement; thus anger is not only useless but harmful.
As for the many other kinds of faults and evils, all should be considered according to principle. Once the principle is clear, the fault will no longer be committed.

What does it mean to reform at the level of the mind? Though faults and evils number thousands and tens of thousands, all are made by the mind. If my mind is not seduced by things, objects, passions, and circumstances into giving rise to bad thoughts, where can faults and evils arise? One who cultivates virtue need not seek out the many faults — lust for beauty, lust for fame, lust for wealth, lust for anger — and reform them one by one by principle or by deed; so long as the right thought of single-minded goodness is present before him, deviant thoughts cannot of themselves defile him. It is like the sun standing in the sky: goblins and spirits all flee into hiding. This is the true transmission of the one that governs the ten thousand! Faults are made by the mind, and so they must also be reformed by the mind, like cutting down a poisonous tree by severing its root directly — why hack at it branch by branch and strip it leaf by leaf?

In sum, the highest method of reforming faults is governing the mind, keeping the mind pure and calm at all times and in all places. Because the mind is pure, as soon as a bad thought stirs it is like a stain on snow-white cloth — one becomes aware of it at once, and the moment one is aware, one clears it away. With no bad thoughts, there will naturally be no bad words or deeds. If one's skill in governing the mind is insufficient, and one cannot yet reach the point where an evil thought 'is noticed the moment it stirs, and vanishes the moment it is noticed,' then one must take up reforming by principle, using reasoned reflection to drive out the fault, as in the examples above of killing living beings and of anger. If reforming by principle is also beyond one, then one must take up reforming by deed, forbidding the deed at once whenever a fault is about to be committed. To practice reforming by mind, which is the higher skill, while also practicing reforming by principle and by deed, which are the lower, is the safest course of all. But to use only the lower skills of reforming by principle and by deed, without understanding how to apply the higher skill of reforming by mind — or even to be ignorant of reforming by principle and know only reforming by deed — is to reform one's faults without enough wisdom.

Yet when one vows to reform one's faults, one must have good friends in this world to remind one when one is confused or slack, and in the unseen realm there must be ghosts and spirits to bear witness. This is because ghosts and spirits have spiritual powers, and all that a person does and thinks is perfectly clear to them; when they attest that you have reformed your faults, then you have truly reformed them. This too is the meaning of the ancients' saying, 'Do not deceive in the dark chamber.' One must repent with a single mind, unremitting day and night; after one seven-day period, two seven-day periods, and on to one month, two months, three months, there will surely be signs of efficacy. Perhaps one feels the mind and spirit at ease and expansive; or feels wisdom suddenly opened; or, amid tangled and tumultuous affairs, suddenly finds thoughts arising that settle everything clearly and neatly; or, meeting enemies and foes, one feels not the least resentment but rather joy in the heart; or one dreams of vomiting black things; or dreams of sages and worthies of old reaching out to guide and receive one; or dreams of flying and strolling through the heavens; or dreams of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. All such excellent things are signs that faults are dissolved and offenses wiped away.
